prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that liquid-liquid phase separation, governed by multivalent interactions, organizes the contents of living cells into membraneless compartments.

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new concept of molecular organisation. Multivalency, phase boundaries, interfacial tension and thermodynamic phase behaviour were used to explain how a cell compartmentalises its chemistry without membranes. The 2009 P-granule work of Brangwynne and Hyman showed liquid-like behaviour in vivo, and the Rosen group's 2012 multivalent-protein work gave the quantitative framework for how valence and affinity set the transition. The idea has since propagated into nucleolar and stress-granule biology, transcription, and the aggregation and amyloid-like maturation that links to neurodegeneration. It is also a field where physical chemistry, rather than synthesis, supplied the explanatory principle. Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen make a clean three-person prize with a defined division between discovery and framework.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit and interpretive maturity. Pappu and Mittag supplied sequence-encoded physical theory and biophysics that are arguably as chemical as the cell-biological demonstrations, and a three-person cut leaves them out. There is also a live debate about which cellular condensates are genuinely equilibrium liquid-liquid phase separation, about in vitro artefacts from overexpression and crowding, and about functional relevance in vivo. A prize would need a citation precise enough not to over-claim, and the opening support (two first places, ranked by only two members) shows it is far from a consensus choice.

responses.point: Linke ranks B001 first for its clear physical principle, phase behaviour applied to compartmentalisation, and asks the committee to probe who first articulated the phase-separation framing versus the later multivalency work.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and share his preferred trio. On his priority question I would credit the 2009 P-granule demonstration to Brangwynne and Hyman as the discovery that cellular compartments behave as liquids, and the 2012 multivalent-polymer work to Rosen as the physical framework explaining how such phases are controlled. These are two linked contributions, not competing priority claims, and both belong in the citation. I would be wary of treating his support and mine as independent confirmation, since we both weigh physical principle heavily.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation (B007) first as a genuinely new modality that converts binding into removal of the target, with clinical-stage degraders and a Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli trio.
responses.response: I take the modality argument seriously and have B007 in my own top three; the ternary-complex thermodynamics and induced-interface chemistry are real physical chemistry. My qualifications concern maturity and attribution. No degrader is approved, so the consequence he requires is still prospective, and the PROTAC strand and the cereblon molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito) are close to two separate discoveries, so any three-name cut is contestable. I would accept B007 if colleagues are comfortable that clinical proof is not yet needed, but I do not think it is clearly ahead of B001 on conceptual novelty.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins (B044, Gray and Winkler) first, as a quantitatively grounded, textbook principle that is overdue, with a clean two-name attribution.
responses.response: I agree this is physical chemistry of the kind I value, and the two-name attribution is an advantage. My reservation is that the underlying electron-transfer theory was already recognised with the Marcus prize, and the protein-tunnelling concept is now so settled that it may read as a retrospective award. Only he ranked it first and nobody else placed it highly. I would ask him what the citation adds beyond Marcus theory; if the answer is mainly experimental verification, I would weigh it below B001, which introduces a new organising idea.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing (B052) first for turning a biological process into a controlled chemical reaction on DNA, and proposes Liu with Komor and Gaudelli.
responses.response: The chemistry is creative and the clinical reach is real, and I would not oppose it. My concern is proximity to the 2020 CRISPR-Cas9 prize: the committee would have to explain why a second genome-editing award is a distinct achievement and not an extension. The Komor and Gaudelli question is also hard, since a Liu-only prize is cleaner but undercredits the trainees he himself names as decisive, while a trio gives away that clarity. Compared with phase separation, I find the conceptual novelty smaller and the attribution more awkward.

responses.point: Zou ranks Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling (B029) first as enormously consequential, a natural two-person prize extending the logic of the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
responses.response: I do not doubt the consequence or the Buchwald and Hartwig attribution, and I accept that it is mature. My difficulty is that, as he notes, it extends the 2010 prize to another bond class, so the conceptual step is smaller than a new organising principle. I would also like the committee to weigh whether synthetic methodology is already well represented relative to physical and biophysical chemistry. I would not call B029 weak, but I would place it behind B001 on originality and treat it as a strong fallback.

uncertainties: Whether the in vivo relevance of condensates as true phase-separated liquids is settled enough to support a Nobel-level citation.
Whether Pappu and Mittag should displace Hyman, Brangwynne or Rosen, or whether the three-person limit makes any allocation unfair.
Whether the committee regards B007 as ready given that no degrader is yet approved, and how PROTAC and molecular-glue credit should be split.
Historical details and priority dates are recalled from memory and have not been verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I share a Lund affiliation with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my lipid self-assembly and amyloid research is scientifically adjacent to B001, but I have no known collaboration with any credited person.
